newsitem.title: USA: Mitsubishi, Jackson group reach deal on discrimination.
newsitem.headline: Mitsubishi, Jackson group reach deal on discrimination.

text.p: Japan's Mitsubishi Motors Corp. said Wednesday it could invest up to $200 million in minority businesses and workers under a deal ending a dispute over alleged racial and sexual discrimination at the company.

Mitsubishi's accord with civil rights leader the Rev. Jesse Jackson's Rainbow/PUSH Coalition ends a boycott called by him because of a 9-month-old sexual discrimination lawsuit filed by female Mitsubishi workers.

"We are determined to create the best possible environment to build the best possible car for our customers," Kohei Ikuta, executive vice president for finance at Mitsubishi Motor Manufacturing of America, told reporters.

Ikuta, flanked by Jackson and National Organisation for Women President Patricia Ireland, added, "I pledge to them, and Mitsubishi Motors pledges to them, to create a workplace environment that is inclusive and just."
Jackson said the accord was part of his group's new focus on opening up U.S. corporations and capital to minorities and women as part of improving economic equality.
The group will open an office in New York's financial district next month to monitor the access of minorities and women to financial resources and jobs.
"There is gold in the ghetto and the barrio, unmined and uncultivated," Jackson said. "Let our talent in -- open up the wall on Wall Street."

The agreement with Mitsubishi comes as minorities and women more and more have publicly alleged patterns of discrimination at big corporations in the United States. NOW's Ireland said only 3 percent to 5 percent of senior executive posts at U.S. companies were filled by minorities and women.
Oil giant Texaco Inc. agreed in November to pay some current and former black employees $176 million in a racial discrimination lawsuit.

This week, two black employees at Morgan Stanley Group Inc. filed a $60 million discrimination lawsuit against the company. They alleged they were passed over for promotions after complaining of racist jokes transmitted via electronic mail.

Under the accord with Mitsubishi, the company's U.S. sales arm, Mitsubishi Motor Sales of America, will boost the number of U.S. dealerships owned by minorities and women to 15 percent over five years. About 10 percent of its 514 dealerships are owned by women, blacks and other minorities.
If the goal is reached, the increase would generate 1,800 to 2,000 new jobs and mean $28 million in capital investments.

The moves also include a stepped-up effort to recruit and train minorities and women to run dealerships. Mitsubishi will set up a programme to ease financial requirements for them to open dealerships and will expand its purchases from minority-owned businesses.
Richard Recchia, chief operating officer of the sales group, said the effort meant "more than $200 million in potential investment to the minority community."
As part of the deal, Mitsubishi Motor Manufacturing agreed to start talks to bring back women on leave or who left work and have filed sexual harassment charges against the company.
The division also will try to determine the facts of the case as quickly as possible and will seek out minority and women vendors for business.

The agreement stems from a federal lawsuit filed by female workers at Mitsubishi's Normal, Ill., plant. They alleged that many female employees were subjected to sexual harassment that the company did nothing to address.
The suit seeks up to $300,000 each for the workers in back pay, benefits and damages.
A spokesman for the federal Equal Employment Opportunity Commission said late Wednesday it was still involved in the lawsuit against Mitsubishi despite the accord.
Asked about the lawsuit, Ikuta said, "We'd like to enable both parties to determine the facts of the case and come to a fair conclusion very soon."
